title: Two Tests, Not One: Bearing Capacity, Settlement and the Rulebooks for a Footing
summary: Every shallow foundation must pass a strength test, bearing capacity, and a stiffness test, settlement, and on soft ground the second usually governs. The footing is governed by the adopted building code, the concrete standard it calls up, and guides that bind only when specified.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a footing can be strong enough and still ruin the building above it. Strength keeps the building up; stiffness keeps it usable, and on soft ground it is stiffness, settlement, that decides the design.

In plain English

A shallow foundation, a pad or strip footing just below ground, spreads a column or wall load over enough soil to carry it. It must pass two separate tests. The first asks whether the soil will shear and fail under the load: that is bearing capacity, a strength test. The second asks how far the footing will sink, and whether neighbouring footings sink by different amounts: that is settlement, a stiffness test. Passing the first says nothing about the second.

Test one: bearing capacity

The ultimate bearing capacity is the pressure at which soil beneath a footing shears and the footing plunges or tilts. Terzaghi's classical method and its later refinements estimate it from the soil's strength, the footing's size and depth, and groundwater. Engineers divide the ultimate value by a factor of safety, commonly quoted around two and a half to three, to give an allowable bearing pressure [unverified — confirm independently]. The geotechnical engineer reports an allowable value for your site; the structural engineer sizes footings so the applied pressure stays below it.

Test two: settlement

Settlement has three parts. Immediate settlement happens as load is applied, mostly from elastic compression. Consolidation settlement happens slowly in saturated clay as water squeezes out under the new load, and can take months or years. Secondary compression continues after that, and is large in organic soils and peat. What damages buildings is mostly differential settlement, the difference between neighbouring points, rather than total settlement. Literature guidance often associates angular distortion, differential settlement divided by the distance between the points, of around 1 in 300 to 1 in 500 with the onset of cracking in partitions and finishes. That is guidance from published studies, not a code limit [unverified — confirm independently].

The options on soft clay

Separate pads on soft clay tend to produce a dish-shaped settlement profile, with interior columns, which carry more load, sinking more than perimeter ones. A mat, one slab under the whole building, bridges between columns and evens movement out. Piles bypass the soft clay and carry load to stronger ground. Preloading, placing a surcharge of fill in advance, often with vertical wick drains to speed drainage, makes the clay consolidate before the building arrives, trading months of programme for certainty. Each is a one-way door once the design is fixed.

Which rulebook governs

Three kinds of document get quoted on foundations. The adopted building code is law. Standards that the code calls up by reference become law through that reference. Guides are good practice only, unless your specification makes them binding.

In the IBC, Chapter 18 governs soils and foundations generally: investigations, presumptive load-bearing values, a requirement to design for settlement as well as capacity, and rules for shallow foundations including minimum depth, commonly quoted at about 12 inches below undisturbed ground [unverified — confirm independently]. ACI 318, called up through IBC Chapter 19, governs the footing as a concrete element: punching shear around the column, one-way shear, flexure and the development of column bars into the footing; its chapter numbering varies by edition. ACI 332 is the residential concrete code and does not belong on an apartment building of consequence. ACI documents with an R suffix, such as 336.2R on mats and 360R and 302.1R on slabs on ground, are guides that bind only when your specification says so. A list of standards in the general notes protects you only if each carries the right edition and the specification makes it enforceable.

A worked example

Suppose a hypothetical soil has an ultimate bearing capacity of 450 kilopascals.

  1. At a factor of safety of 3, the allowable bearing pressure is 450 divided by 3, which is 150 kilopascals.
  2. A column load of 1,800 kilonewtons needs a footing area of 1,800 divided by 150, which is 12 square metres, a pad about 3.5 metres square. The strength test passes by design.
  3. Now the second test. Suppose the geotechnical engineer estimates 70 millimetres of settlement for that pad and 45 millimetres for a smaller neighbouring pad 6 metres away.
  4. Differential settlement is 25 millimetres over 6,000 millimetres: 1 in 240.
  5. Against guidance of 1 in 300 to 1 in 500, that is worse than the cracking threshold. Both pads pass bearing; the building fails the stiffness test.

Time is part of the answer

Consolidation settlement in clay is slow, because water has to drain out of tiny pores before the clay compresses. A building on clay may show little movement at handover and a great deal over the following years. So a settlement estimate should come with a time estimate: how much happens during construction, when finishes are not yet fixed, and how much after, when it cracks plaster and moves door frames. A design that keeps most settlement inside the construction period, by preloading or by sequencing, can tolerate a larger total than one where it arrives after occupation.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a foundation report that gives an allowable bearing pressure and no settlement estimate. It answers the easier question and leaves the one that governs on soft ground unanswered.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hears "the footings pass bearing" and considers the foundation design settled. He also accepts a general notes list of standards without editions, or one that names ACI 332 or an undated guide, both of which are defects.

How you will use it

Require both tests in writing: an allowable bearing pressure and settlement estimates, total and differential, for the actual footing layout. Ask what angular distortion the design predicts and what limit the engineer is designing to. Check that the standards list names editions and that guides are made binding by the specification where you rely on them. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer and structural engineer of record.
checklist: Require an allowable bearing pressure and settlement estimates, both in writing.
Ask for predicted differential settlement and angular distortion between columns.
Ask what distortion limit the engineers are designing to and where it comes from.
Decline presumptive bearing values on a building of consequence.
Check that every standard in the general notes carries an edition.
Make sure ACI 332 does not appear on a building of consequence.
Make guides binding through the specification where you rely on them.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: The geotechnical report gives an allowable bearing pressure of 150 kilopascals and says nothing about settlement. The structural engineer has sized every pad to it. Is the foundation design complete?
selftest.a: No. Only the strength test has been done. On compressible ground the settlement test usually governs, so you need total and differential settlement estimates for the actual footing layout and a check of angular distortion against the design limit. Ask the geotechnical engineer for them before the design is fixed.

apply: For two hypothetical pads 7 metres apart settling 80 and 55 millimetres, compute the angular distortion and compare it with 1 in 300 and 1 in 500.
sources: Terzaghi bearing capacity theory and consolidation theory are standard geotechnical engineering. IBC Chapter 18 and 19, ACI 318, ACI 332, ACI 336.2R, 360R and 302.1R as commonly cited; section numbers, minimum depths and factors of safety vary by edition [unverified — confirm independently]. Distortion limits are literature guidance, not code. Example hypothetical.

title: When the Ground Says No: Foundation Failures in Strength and Stiffness
summary: Foundation failures fall into four families: bearing capacity failure, excessive total settlement, differential settlement, and disturbance from outside. Transcona, Pisa, Kansai, Lotus Riverside and Mexico City's cathedral each show one of them, and the organisational thread is treating cracks as separate defects.
body:
Mr Shabazz, foundations rarely fail in a single dramatic moment; most fail slowly, and the evidence arrives as small, separate-looking defects. The famous cases are worth knowing because each one isolates a single way the ground says no.

In plain English

A foundation fails when the ground either cannot carry the load, which is a strength failure, or moves too much, which is a stiffness failure. Sometimes something outside the building disturbs the ground it sits on. Each family has a different signature, and recognising the signature tells you what kind of problem you have.

The four families

First, bearing capacity failure: the soil shears, and the foundation plunges or rotates, sometimes suddenly. Second, excessive total settlement: the whole building sinks further than services, entrances and neighbours can tolerate. Third, differential settlement: parts of the building sink by different amounts, cracking walls, jamming doors and tilting floors. Fourth, disturbance from outside: excavation, dewatering, vibration or heavy loading next door changes the ground under a building that was performing well.

The cases

Transcona Grain Elevator, near Winnipeg, October 1913. A strong concrete structure on a mat over clay was filled with grain quickly for the first time and rotated to roughly 27 degrees as the clay beneath it failed. It was later underpinned and brought back near vertical. The lesson: a sound structure on ground loaded close to its ultimate capacity, fast, fails in bearing.

The bell tower at Pisa. It began to tilt during construction, by around the third storey, on soft ground. A long pause in construction, for reasons unrelated to engineering, gave the clay time to consolidate and gain strength, which probably saved it. It was closed in 1990, stabilised by carefully extracting soil from beneath the high side, and reopened in 2001. The lesson: time changes soft clay, and controlled soil removal can correct a tilt.

Kansai International Airport, Osaka Bay, opened 1994. Built on an artificial island over deep soft clay, it settled more than original predictions, although the terminal was designed with jackable column supports so it could be relevelled. The lesson: where settlement is uncertain, you can buy optionality in concrete and steel.

Lotus Riverside, Shanghai, June 2009. A newly built thirteen-storey residential building on piles toppled. As the investigation was widely reported, excavation had been carried out on one side while a high stockpile of soil was placed on the other, and the lateral pressure difference failed the piles. The lesson: work next to a finished building can destroy it.

The Metropolitan Cathedral, Mexico City. Built over roughly two and a half centuries on soft lake clay, it distorted through differential settlement, which was worsened in the twentieth century by groundwater extraction across the city. It was stabilised in the 1990s by controlled under-excavation. The lesson: settlement on soft clay has a long memory, and changes after completion, such as falling groundwater, can restart it.

All five are summarised from public accounts and investigations. Read the primary sources before quoting figures.

A worked example

Suppose a hypothetical apartment building, two years after completion, generates these reports from one corner:

  1. A tenant reports a door that sticks in a ground-floor unit.
  2. Maintenance reports a diagonal crack above a window two floors up, on the same line of columns.
  3. The lift contractor reports that the car needed adjustment twice at that end.
  4. A level survey would show the corner column about 30 millimetres lower than its neighbour 6 metres away: 1 in 200.
  5. Three reports, one cause: differential settlement at that corner, perhaps over a thicker pocket of soft clay. Repairing the door, the crack and the lift separately treats symptoms and lets the cause continue.
  6. The correct response is a monitoring survey over time to see whether movement is continuing, a geotechnical review of the ground at that corner, and only then a repair strategy.

The organisational thread

Two habits recur. Treating the ground as a fixed input, when it responds to time, loading, water and neighbours. And explaining away cracks, sticking doors and lift adjustments as separate defects, assigned to separate trades, so nobody connects them until the pattern is expensive. Inversion helps: ask what single cause would explain all the complaints at once.

What each case says to an owner

Read together, the cases make a short list of questions for any project on soft ground. How close to its ultimate capacity will the ground be loaded, and how fast? How long will the clay take to consolidate, and is there time in the programme for it? If settlement is uncertain, can the building be designed to tolerate or correct it, as Kansai's columns were? What could neighbours do to the ground beside us, and do we have rights or monitoring to protect against it? And what could change the groundwater after we finish? Each question maps to one case, and each has a cheap answer at design stage and an expensive one later.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is fragmented reporting. When each symptom goes to a different trade for repair, nobody with authority over the whole building sees the pattern.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes a building that performed well for years is safe from foundation movement. Groundwater changes, new excavation next door or a heavy stockpile can change the ground beneath it at any time.

How you will use it

Log every crack, sticking door and lift adjustment by location, and look for clusters. Install settlement points on new buildings and read them through the first years. Monitor neighbouring work, including excavation and stockpiles, against your building. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer and structural engineer for any investigation or repair.
checklist: Log cracks, sticking doors and lift adjustments by location and look for clusters.
Treat symptoms in one zone as one finding until proven otherwise.
Install settlement points and read them through the first years after completion.
Watch neighbouring excavation, dewatering and stockpiles near your building.
Ask whether groundwater levels in the area are changing.
Investigate the cause before repairing the symptoms.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A year after handover, one corner of a building produces a cracked partition, a sticking door and a lift that needed adjusting. The contractor proposes three separate repairs. What do you do?
selftest.a: Treat it as one finding, probably differential settlement in that zone, until proven otherwise. Commission a level survey and settlement monitoring over time to see whether movement is continuing, and a geotechnical review of the ground there. Repair the symptoms only once the cause and its trend are known.

apply: Look at any building you know with a visible crack and write down which of the four failure families it might belong to and what you would measure to tell.
sources: Transcona Grain Elevator (1913), the bell tower at Pisa, Kansai International Airport, Lotus Riverside (Shanghai, 2009) and the Metropolitan Cathedral of Mexico City are summarised from public accounts and published investigations; read primary sources before quoting figures. Example hypothetical and composite.

title: Sizing a Pad Footing: The Bearing Check Passes, the Settlement Check Decides
summary: A worked pad footing shows that a correctly sized footing passes its bearing check, while the settlement calculation shows the building failing its distortion limit. Enlarging footings helps until their stressed zones overlap, which is the point to price a mat, ground improvement or piles.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this lesson runs both foundation tests on one hypothetical building, step by step. Both footings pass bearing, and the building still fails, which is the whole argument for asking for settlement figures.

In plain English

Sizing a footing starts with the load each column carries, divides it by the allowable bearing pressure to get an area, then adds the weight of the footing itself and checks again. Settlement is then estimated by working out how much extra stress the footing puts into the clay below, and how much the clay compresses under it. All numbers here are illustrative and simplified; the real design belongs to the engineers.

The building

A hypothetical flat-plate frame with four supported floor levels on an 8 by 8 metre column grid, carrying about 9 kilonewtons per square metre of service load per level, including self-weight. Footings sit 1.2 metres below ground. The allowable bearing pressure is 200 kilopascals. Beneath the footings is a 4-metre layer of soft clay starting about 1.5 metres below footing level.

A worked example

  1. Interior column load: tributary area 8 times 8, 64 square metres, times 9 kilonewtons per square metre times 4 levels, is about 2,304 kilonewtons. A perimeter column carries about half: 1,152 kilonewtons.
  2. First guess for the interior pad: 2,304 divided by 200 is 11.5 square metres, a pad about 3.4 metres square.
  3. Add the footing's own weight. A 3.4 metre pad, 0.7 metres thick, at 24 kilonewtons per cubic metre, weighs about 194 kilonewtons. Pressure becomes 2,498 divided by 11.56, about 216 kilopascals. That fails.
  4. Try 3.6 metres: area 12.96 square metres, weight about 218 kilonewtons, pressure about 195 kilopascals. That passes.
  5. Perimeter pad of 2.6 metres: area 6.76 square metres, weight about 114 kilonewtons, pressure about 187 kilopascals. That passes too.
  6. Net pressure: excavating 1.2 metres of soil at about 18 kilonewtons per cubic metre removes about 21.6 kilopascals of existing load, so the net added pressures are about 173 kilopascals interior and about 166 perimeter.
  7. Stress at depth, by the simple 2-to-1 spread method, which spreads load one unit outward for every two units down: at mid-clay, 3.5 metres below the footing, the interior pad adds about 173 times 12.96 divided by 7.1 squared, about 44 kilopascals. The perimeter pad adds about 30.
  8. Consolidation: with an existing effective stress at mid-clay of about 60 kilopascals, a compression index of 0.35, an initial void ratio of 1.0 and a layer 4 metres thick, settlement is the thickness times the compression index, divided by one plus the void ratio, times the logarithm of final over initial stress. Interior: about 169 millimetres. Perimeter: about 124 millimetres.
  9. Differential: 45 millimetres over 8 metres, about 1 in 180. Against literature guidance of 1 in 300 to 1 in 500 for the onset of cracking, that is well over. Both footings pass bearing; the building fails.

Trying a bigger interior pad

Enlarge the interior pad to 5 metres. Its weight rises to about 420 kilonewtons, but its pressure falls to about 109 kilopascals gross and 87 net. Added stress at mid-clay falls to about 30 kilopascals, the same as the perimeter pad, and settlement falls to about 124 millimetres. The differential nearly disappears.

But 5-metre pads on an 8-metre grid leave only 3 metres between footings, and their stressed zones overlap at depth, so each footing feels its neighbours' load and the simple calculation understates settlement. Total settlement of over 120 millimetres also remains a problem for services, ramps and thresholds. This is the point to price a mat, ground improvement such as preloading with wick drains, or piles.

What the numbers teach

The bearing factor of safety did its job and protected against shear failure. It did nothing for settlement. On soft clay, footing size is decided by the stiffness test, and when footings grow until they nearly touch, the foundation type itself should be reconsidered.

The structural checks inside the footing

Once the plan size is set by the ground, the footing must also work as concrete. The structural engineer checks punching shear around the column, where the column tries to push through the pad; one-way shear across the pad's width; bending, which sets the bottom reinforcement; and the development length of the column bars anchored into the footing. These checks set the thickness, here 0.7 metres, which is why thickness and plan size are designed together. A thicker pad weighs more, which feeds back into the bearing check, so the sizing is an iteration rather than a single calculation.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is approving a footing layout on bearing alone, then discovering the differential settlement after the frame is built, when the only options are expensive.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner forgets the footing's own weight and the soil it replaces. Here, footing weight turned a pass into a fail; net pressure then changed the settlement figures. Both belong in the check.

How you will use it

Ask for the bearing check with footing weight included, the net pressure, the settlement estimate for interior and perimeter footings, and the resulting angular distortion. If footings grow until they are nearly touching, ask for a mat, ground improvement and piles to be priced side by side. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer for settlement; structural engineer of record for sizing.
checklist: Include the footing's own weight in the bearing check.
Use net pressure, after removing excavated soil, for settlement.
Ask for settlement of interior and perimeter footings separately.
Compute angular distortion between neighbouring columns.
Watch for footings growing until their stressed zones overlap.
Price a mat, ground improvement and piles side by side when pads become very large.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A design shows interior pads settling 150 millimetres and perimeter pads 110 millimetres, 7.5 metres apart, with all pads passing bearing. What do you conclude?
selftest.a: Differential settlement is 40 millimetres over 7,500 millimetres, about 1 in 190, worse than the 1 in 300 to 1 in 500 cracking guidance. The bearing check passing does not protect against that. Ask whether enlarging pads is practical without overlapping stressed zones, and have a mat, ground improvement and piles priced, given that total settlement is also large.

apply: Repeat the interior pad bearing check for an allowable pressure of 180 kilopascals, including the footing's weight, and find the smallest whole-tenth pad size that passes.
sources: Pad sizing, the 2-to-1 stress spread approximation and one-dimensional consolidation are standard simplified geotechnical methods; real designs use more rigorous analysis. Soil parameters, loads and distortion guidance are illustrative and literature-based, not code [unverified — confirm independently]. All figures hypothetical.

title: One Slab Under the Whole Building: Mats, Compensation and Uplift
summary: A mat shares load across the whole footprint, lowers bearing pressure and evens out differential settlement, but it does not by itself stop total settlement on deep soft clay. Digging deeper can compensate the load, at the price of uplift that must be resisted before the pumps may stop.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a mat solves evenness more reliably than it solves total settlement. And the trick of digging deeper to cancel the building's weight works on the soil while making the water problem worse.

In plain English

A mat, or raft, is one thick reinforced slab under the whole building. It spreads load over the entire footprint, so the bearing pressure is low, and because it is stiff it bridges over soft spots, so neighbouring columns settle by similar amounts. It also gives you a lowest floor. What it does not automatically do is stop the building sinking as a whole, because a large loaded area stresses the ground to a much greater depth than a small pad.

How a mat is analysed

A rigid analysis treats the mat as infinitely stiff and gives a first answer for pressure. A flexible analysis puts the mat on springs representing the soil, and the stiffness of those springs, the modulus of subgrade reaction, is not a fixed soil property: it depends on the mat's size and on how long the load acts. So the geotechnical and structural engineers have to iterate it together, each adjusting to the other's results. In American practice the mat is governed by IBC Chapter 18 for foundations, ACI 318 through IBC Chapter 19 for the concrete, and ACI 336.2R as a guide that binds only if specified [unverified — confirm independently]. The checks that catch people out are punching shear at heavily loaded columns and permanent uplift below the water table.

A worked example

Use the same hypothetical building as yesterday: four supported levels at about 9 kilonewtons per square metre, on a mat 32 by 24 metres, 768 square metres.

  1. Building load: 4 times 9 is 36 kilopascals. Mat self-weight at 0.8 metres thick and 24 kilonewtons per cubic metre: 19.2 kilopascals. Gross pressure: about 55 kilopascals, against about 195 under yesterday's interior pad.
  2. Excavating 1.5 metres of soil at 18 kilonewtons per cubic metre removes 27 kilopascals. Net pressure: about 28 kilopascals.
  3. Stress at mid-clay, 3.5 metres below the mat, by the 2-to-1 method: 28.2 times 768 divided by 27.5 times 35.5, about 22 kilopascals. Settlement with yesterday's clay parameters: about 96 millimetres, spread evenly under the building rather than dished.
  4. Now look deeper. At 10 metres below the base, the mat still adds about 15 kilopascals, while yesterday's interior pad added only about 12. A big loaded area reaches deeper ground, so if there is more soft clay down there, the mat's total settlement can exceed what the pads would have produced.

Compensation

Dig deeper and you remove more soil weight. At about 3 metres deep, the soil removed weighs about 54 kilopascals, nearly equal to the gross pressure, and the net added pressure approaches zero. That is a compensated foundation: the building replaces the soil it displaced, and in principle the clay feels little change.

The price: uplift

  1. Suppose the design groundwater level is 0.5 metres below grade.
  2. Shallow mat, base at 1.5 metres: head of 1.0 metre, about 10 kilopascals of uplift. Mat weight counted at a reduced dead-load factor of 0.9, as load combinations commonly require for resisting uplift, is 0.9 times 19.2, about 17.3 kilopascals [unverified — confirm independently]. It stays down even when empty.
  3. Deep compensated mat, base at 3 metres: head of 2.5 metres, about 25 kilopascals. Against 17.3 of factored mat weight, the empty mat would float.
  4. Each floor level adds perhaps 6 kilopascals of dead load, about 5.4 when factored. The shortfall of about 7.7 kilopascals needs about 1.4 levels, so in practice two floor levels must be built before the pumps may stop, unless the mat is anchored.
  5. That crossover date belongs in the programme, certified in writing by the engineer of record, not set by the dewatering contractor's hire period.

Applied: a tilting mat

If the soft clay is thicker under one corner of the footprint, a mat turns individual dishes under each column into a gentle tilt of the whole building. Ask the lift supplier early what plumb tolerance his rails need, because a tilt the structure tolerates easily may be too much for a lift. If movement is still too large, the next options are ground improvement, a piled raft where piles carry part of the load, or full piles.

The construction side

A mat is a single large concrete placement under every column, over a waterproofing membrane that will never be seen again once concrete covers it. That makes its construction a set of decisions that close on one day: the membrane is accepted or not, the reinforcement is released or not, and the pour is either continuous or broken at joints the engineer has located. The next week's lessons cover the pour itself, but the design should already state how the mat will be placed, because pour joints, cooling and access for concrete trucks are design questions as well as site ones.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a deep mat in wet ground whose pumps stop on the programme date rather than the certified crossover. An empty, buoyant mat can lift, crack or tilt.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hears that a mat cuts bearing pressure by two thirds and assumes settlement falls in proportion. Bearing pressure and settlement answer different questions, and settlement depends on how deep the stress reaches.

How you will use it

Ask for mat settlement estimates that include deeper strata, not only the layer under a pad. Ask how the modulus of subgrade reaction was agreed between the two engineers. Ask for the uplift check in the empty condition and the certified date pumps may stop. Ask the lift supplier for his tolerance. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer and structural engineer of record.
checklist: Ask for mat settlement estimates that include deeper soft strata.
Ask how the modulus of subgrade reaction was agreed between the two engineers.
Check punching shear at heavily loaded columns.
Ask for the uplift check with the building empty.
Get the date pumps may stop certified in writing by the engineer of record.
Ask the lift supplier early for his plumb tolerance.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Your engineer proposes deepening the mat to compensate the building's load, which cuts net pressure almost to zero. The water table is near the surface. What must you ask?
selftest.a: Ask for the uplift check in the empty condition: a deeper base sees more water head, and the mat's own factored weight may not resist it, so the structure could float until enough floors are built or the mat is anchored. Ask when pumping may stop and require that crossover certified in writing. Also ask whether deeper strata change the settlement picture.

apply: For a mat 0.9 metres thick with its base 2 metres below a water table, compute uplift, the mat's weight at a 0.9 factor, and whether it floats when empty.
sources: Mat analysis approaches and the modulus of subgrade reaction follow standard geotechnical and structural practice. IBC Chapters 18 and 19, ACI 318 and ACI 336.2R as commonly cited; the reduced dead-load factor follows ASCE 7 load combinations as commonly quoted [unverified — confirm independently]. All figures hypothetical and simplified.

title: Week Seven Review: Two Tests, One Building
summary: Six scenario questions on bearing capacity and settlement, the rulebooks that govern a footing, foundation failure patterns, footing sizing and mats. The week's thread is that strength keeps the building up, stiffness keeps it usable, and on soft ground stiffness decides.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week separated the two questions every foundation must answer. Work through each question aloud before reading the answer.

Question 1. A report gives an allowable bearing pressure but no settlement estimate. What is missing, and why does it matter?

Answer. Only the strength test has been answered. Settlement, the stiffness test, is missing, and on compressible ground it usually governs the design. Ask for total and differential settlement estimates for the actual footing layout, and the predicted angular distortion between neighbouring columns.

As you work through these, watch how often the right answer is a request for a missing number rather than a calculation of your own: a settlement estimate, a distortion limit, a certified date. The owner's job on foundations is mostly to notice which test has not been run.

Question 2. The general notes list "ACI 332" and "ACI 336.2R" with no editions for a mid-rise apartment building. What is wrong?

Answer. ACI 332 is the residential concrete code and does not belong on a building of this kind; the footing is governed by ACI 318 through the adopted building code. ACI 336.2R is a guide that binds only if the specification makes it binding, and without an edition it is unenforceable in any case. Both are defects to correct.

Question 3. In one corner of a two-year-old building, a partition cracks, a door sticks and the lift needs adjusting. Three reports or one?

Answer. Treat them as one finding, probably differential settlement in that zone, until proven otherwise. Commission a level survey and monitoring over time, and a geotechnical review of the ground there, before any repair. Repairing the symptoms separately lets the cause continue.

Question 4. Interior pads are estimated to settle 169 millimetres and perimeter pads 124 millimetres, 8 metres apart. Both pass bearing. Does the building pass?

Answer. No. The differential is 45 millimetres over 8,000 millimetres, about 1 in 180, worse than the 1 in 300 to 1 in 500 cracking guidance from the literature. Bearing passing does not protect against settlement. Enlarging interior pads helps until their stressed zones overlap; at that point price a mat, ground improvement and piles.

Question 5. A mat cuts net bearing pressure by more than 80 percent compared with the interior pads. Will settlement fall by the same proportion?

Answer. Not necessarily. A large loaded area stresses the ground much deeper than a pad, so at 10 metres down the mat may add more stress than the pad did. A mat reliably buys evenness; total settlement depends on the deeper strata. Ask for settlement estimates that include them.

Question 6. A compensated mat 3 metres deep sits below a water table 0.5 metres below grade. The programme shows dewatering ending when the mat is complete. Is that safe?

Answer. Probably not. A head of 2.5 metres gives about 25 kilopascals of uplift, while an 0.8 metre mat counted at a reduced dead-load factor provides only about 17. The empty mat would float. Pumping must continue until enough floors are built, roughly two levels on these numbers, or the mat is anchored, and the engineer of record certifies the crossover in writing.

Recap

Every shallow foundation passes two tests. Bearing capacity, the strength test, divides the ultimate capacity by a factor of safety. Settlement, the stiffness test, adds immediate, consolidation and secondary compression, and what damages buildings is differential settlement. On soft ground the second test decides.

The code governs the ground, the referenced concrete standard governs the footing as concrete, and guides bind only when specified. Editions matter, and the residential code does not belong on an apartment building.

Foundation failures come in four families: bearing failure, total settlement, differential settlement and outside disturbance. Transcona, Pisa, Kansai, Lotus Riverside and Mexico City's cathedral each show one. The human failure is treating ground as fixed and cracks as separate defects.

Sizing a pad includes its own weight; settlement uses net pressure and stress at depth. Both footings can pass bearing while the building fails on distortion.

A mat buys evenness, a lowest floor and low bearing pressure, but reaches deeper ground. Compensation reduces net load and increases uplift, so the pumps stop on a certified date.

The thread: strength keeps the building up; stiffness keeps it usable; on soft ground the second decides. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer and structural engineer of record.

The habit to keep from this week is short. Whenever someone tells you a foundation passes, ask which test: strength, stiffness, or both, and over what time. Then ask what single cause would explain any complaints that arrive after handover. Those two questions catch most of what goes wrong below ground before it becomes expensive.

Next week finishes the course at the lowest floor: what water does to a slab below the water table, how a large mat is poured in one go, and the ground slab that carries the tenants, from its subgrade to the moisture test that releases the flooring.
checklist: Ask for both the bearing and settlement tests in writing.
Check standards lists for editions and wrong codes.
Treat clustered symptoms as one finding.
Include footing weight and net pressure in any check.
Ask for mat settlement including deeper strata.
Get the pumps-off date certified for any mat below the water table.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Why can enlarging pad footings stop helping on soft clay?
selftest.a: Because once pads grow until they are close together, their stressed zones overlap at depth, so each footing feels its neighbours' loads and the building behaves more like a loaded mat, with large total settlement. At that point the foundation type, a mat, ground improvement or piles, should be reconsidered and priced.
